column3: It is the closest verbal parallel: on that day the wrongdoers' excuse does not benefit them.
It contrasts the same day, when truthful people benefit from their truth and receive mutual good pleasure.
It states that wrongdoers gain no benefit that day even by sharing punishment.
It directly parallels the irreversible threshold: faith then no longer benefits disbelievers and they receive no delay.
The immediate context shows the guilty making a false claim when the Hour rises, preparing the denial of their excuse.
It depicts wrongdoers finally confessing their injustice, a confession that comes too late to alter the outcome.
It closely repeats the judicial setting: witnesses appear, disbelievers are not permitted, and are not allowed to seek redress.
The verse immediately before the focus identifies the day as resurrection and exposes their prior lack of knowledge.
It closely parallels the refusal of restored favor after punishment has become their settled abode.
Its same-day formula and absence of questioning present a distinct mode of final judgment.
It identifies the guilty as already in error and burning punishment, but adds little to excuse or redress.
The pairing of excuse and warning helps distinguish a timely warning from the later useless excuse.
It directly shows the final closure of apologetic speech: they are not permitted to offer excuses.
The following exhortation to patience rests on the certainty of God's promise but does not explain the barred excuse.
It repeats that those in the Fire neither leave it nor are allowed to seek restored favor.
It supplies the nearby judgment sequence in which the wrongdoers see punishment and receive neither relief nor respite.
A nearby statement of inability to make the rejecting hear complements their prior unresponsiveness, not the final judicial closure.
The contrast of darkness and light does not materially clarify excuses or redress on the Day.

The mention of an inscribed book alone adds no clear interpretive value here.
It contrasts present reminder that benefits believers with the focus's point at which response is no longer useful.
It gives another Day when ordinary assets provide no benefit, broadening the focus's final loss of recourse.

Return to God establishes the resurrection horizon but is less specific than the surrounding verses.
Worldly benefits and gratitude do not clarify the final ineffectiveness of excuses.
The command not to plead concerning doomed wrongdoers supplies a historical counterpart to barred post-verdict intercession.
The challenge to present a clear thing has no meaningful link to the focus.
The incapacity of false objects to benefit or harm concerns idolatry rather than final excuses.

It states that wrongdoers meet the consequences of what they earned, without explaining the closed avenues of response.
The Roman defeat announcement adds no value to the focus.
Deliverance from darkness through clear signs concerns prior guidance, not the final denial of excuse.
It explicitly teaches that faith acquired at the decisive sign no longer benefits, clarifying the focus's time-bound closure.

Its warning that wrongdoers do not prosper concerns eventual outcome but not the focus's judicial closure.
It portrays excuses as unable to override a person's own self-witness, clarifying why an excuse cannot avail.

Rescue of the God-conscious does not illuminate the focus's treatment of wrongdoers.
The forecast of Roman victory is unrelated to the focus.
It states the Day's perfect non-injustice and exact recompense, grounding the justice of the focus's final refusal.
Perpetual punishment without relief or delay loosely parallels finality, but not excuse or redress specifically.
The sign in sleep and seeking bounty does not clarify the focus.
The question about powerless objects concerns idolatry and only shares the language of benefit and harm.
Unrelieved punishment and no respite provide a broad parallel to finality only.
The demand for the decisive opening forms the immediate question answered by the next verse's no-benefit threshold.
It insists that recompense is not wrongful but follows what hands sent ahead, supporting the focus's address to wrongdoers.
It affirms that repentance or punishment lies with God, but does not locate the final closure described here.
The certainty of God's promise supports the surah's judgment horizon without adding to the focus's terms.
The test of whether idols benefit or harm is a distant thematic parallel only.
It depicts a Day with no transferable protection, ransom, intercession, or help, complementing the focus's failed excuse.
The signs in winds, sailing, bounty, and gratitude do not clarify the focus.
Warning wrongdoers before the outcome only broadly contrasts with their later lack of recourse.
Its Day-of-Judgment warning removes substitute payment, intercession, and help, adding personal accountability alongside the focus.
God's final separation among communities on the Day provides the adjudicative setting for the focus.
A historical destruction of wrongdoers supplies only a general pattern of earned consequence.
The description of treaty-breaking aggressors does not clarify the focus.
The call to glorify God at set times has no material link to the focus.
It affirms that warning and destruction are not wrongful, but remains remote from excuse and redress.
The disbelievers' inability to ward off Fire is a broad final-punishment parallel.
The sign in winds and rain does not clarify the focus.
It identifies deniers of clear signs as wrongdoers, giving prior culpability but not the final response.
It states that on that Day no one can control benefit or harm for another, a close parallel to failed recourse for wrongdoers.
Pilgrimage benefits and remembrance do not illuminate the focus.
The sudden approach of the true promise brings a late admission that the deniers were wrongdoers.
No mitigation or help for those preferring worldly life offers only a general image of irrevocable punishment.
Praise at cosmic times does not add interpretive value for the focus.
The announced destruction of a wrongdoing town gives a historical consequence, not the focus's judicial mechanism.
Its use of excuse as a pre-judgment duty before God provides a contrast to the later useless excuse.
The surah's earlier appeal to prior peoples shows clear messengers and self-inflicted wrongdoing before the final outcome.
It sharply contrasts the focus: timely faith benefited Jonah's people, whereas response after the decisive threshold does not.
Reward and freedom from fear for charitable believers do not clarify the focus.
It anticipates recompense according to earnings, but does not address excuse or restoration.
The Flood after prolonged warning is a broad historical pattern of overdue judgment.
The reward for untainted charity does not clarify the focus.
The introduction to a town parable does not by itself add value here.
It explicitly denies divine wrongdoing and attributes the outcome to their own wrongdoing, supporting the focus's justice.
The command not to make excuses because disbelief has occurred directly illustrates an excuse that cannot undo culpable action.
Adam's boundary in the garden does not materially clarify the focus's final judgment.
It calls for action before a Day without exchange, friendship, or intercession, explaining the temporal urgency behind the focus.
The suddenness that prevents a final testament or return only broadly resembles lost opportunity.
It links association with final exclusion and lack of helpers for wrongdoers, but not the focus's excuse or redress.
The curse, deafness, and blindness do not add a specific interpretive link.
The shared enduring Fire as recompense for wrongdoers is a general final-consequence parallel.
The question about a share of dominion is unrelated to the focus.
Clear verses leading believers from darkness to light concern prior guidance, not final excuses.
It traces present wrongdoing back to the self and then to return and report before God, but remains indirect.
The Book, witnesses, true judgment, and absence of injustice supply a detailed courtroom setting for the focus's closure.
It names association as grave wrongdoing, explaining the class addressed by the focus only in a general way.
The warning about consuming orphan property does not clarify the focus's excuse or denied redress.
It sets the same terminal boundary: repentance is not accepted when death arrives and the person says, "now I repent."
On that Day the disbelievers cannot conceal any statement from God, supporting the focus's futility of later defense.
The wrongdoers' wish to be returned after seeing the Fire portrays a belated attempt to reverse their settled outcome.
Those who denied the meeting with God regret their loss when the Hour arrives suddenly, clarifying the shock of final accountability.
When the realization arrives, former deniers ask for intercessors or return, a direct counterpart to the focus's closed recourse.
Every wrongdoing soul would offer ransom after seeing punishment and conceals regret when judgment is made in justice.
Wrongdoers facing punishment ask for a short delay to answer the call, an explicit late plea that illuminates the focus's refusal.
Seeing the Fire, the guilty know they will enter it and find no diversion from it, reinforcing the irreversible outcome.
All faces are humbled before the Living Sustainer, and whoever bears wrongdoing fails, supplying the Day's posture of accountability.
At death the wrongdoer asks to be returned, making explicit the late request for another opportunity before its final refusal.
It denies the requested return and places a barrier until resurrection, directly clarifying that the missed time cannot be reopened.
The wrongdoer bites his hands on the Day and regrets not taking the Messenger's way, a vivid late recognition of culpability.
The guilty lower their heads before their Lord, confessing that they now see and hear and asking to be returned for righteous action.
Those crying in the Fire ask to be brought out to act rightly, but are answered that their allotted time and warning were already given.
It voices the soul's regret for neglecting its duty toward God, directly portraying the belated self-excuse behind the focus.
The wish for another chance after seeing punishment shows the futile desire to resume the period for righteous action.
God answers that clear signs had already come and were denied, explaining why the subsequent regret cannot avail.
Those who disbelieved call for death after being summoned from death to life, revealing the final despair after judgment.
Their double-death confession acknowledges sins and asks whether any way out remains, a direct analogue to barred redress.
The answer grounds their fate in prior disbelief and association when God alone was invoked, explaining the final closure.
Those whom God leaves astray have no protector, and wrongdoers seeing punishment ask whether there is any way of return.
At the final encounter the companion is wished to be at the distance of east and west, expressing irreversible regret immediately before 43:39.
The condemned companion rejects blame and recalls prior warning, framing the judgment as settled responsibility rather than a viable excuse.
On the Day of punishment, the guilty person would wish to ransom himself with his children, another failed avenue of escape.
The guilty person's wish to ransom himself with spouse and brother extends the focus's picture of futile last recourse.
Even clan and all people on earth are imagined as ransom, emphasizing that no substitute can reopen the verdict.
The wish that everything on earth might save the guilty person completes the passage's absolute failure of ransom.
It states that no intercession of intercessors benefits them, closely complementing the focus's no-benefit formula.
It identifies the Day when they will not speak, providing the broader procedural closure for 77:36 and the focus.
Its woe to deniers after the barred-excuse scene reinforces the finality of the judgment.
On the Day no one speaks except by permission and with what is right, closely supporting the focus's denial of later defense.
When the overwhelming event comes and a person remembers what he strove for, it supplies the retrospective setting of accountability.
The Day when one flees from his brother depicts the collapse of ordinary human support at final judgment.
Flight from mother and father further shows that no familial recourse remains on that Day.
Flight from spouse and children completes the loss of ordinary relational support relevant to the focus's denied redress.
Each person has a concern sufficient for him that Day, explaining why no outside remedy or advocacy is available.
It defines the Day as one in which no soul can do anything for another and all command belongs to God, a close parallel to failed recourse.
Leaders and followers disown one another after seeing punishment and severed ties, showing the collapse of hoped-for support.
The followers wish they could return to disown their leaders, but their deeds are shown as irreversible regrets and they cannot leave the Fire.
No earth-full ransom of gold is accepted from those who die rejecting faith, supplying a related limit on late compensation.
When all are gathered, those who associated partners are challenged about their claimed associates, exposing failed defense at judgment.
Their final plea that they were not associators shows a futile attempt at self-exculpation before God.
At the collective appearance before God, the weak appeal to leaders, who deny any power to save and declare panic and patience alike futile.
Those who associated partners see their claimed partners and make a defensive declaration, which their partners immediately reject.
On that Day they offer submission to God and their fabricated claims disappear, a counterpart to the focus's ineffective excuse.
It explicitly names the Day of Regret, when the matter is decided while people had been heedless and unbelieving.
On the Day all follow the Caller without deviation and voices are humbled, depicting a setting with no independent maneuvering.
The just scales of resurrection leave no soul wronged and bring every deed to account, grounding the final verdict's justice.
When the Trumpet is blown, lineage no longer operates among them and they do not ask about one another, removing ordinary relational recourse.
Those with heavy scales prosper, providing the positive counterpart to the focus's wrongdoers at final reckoning.
Those with light scales lose themselves and remain in Hell, clarifying the consequence of failed accountability.
The people of the Fire wish for a return so they could become believers, a direct late request for another opportunity.
The passage follows that regret with the sign and the observation that most still would not believe, explaining the prior refusal.
On the Day God calls the associators to produce their claimed partners, exposing a failed defense at the judgment.
Those against whom the word is due admit they led others astray and dissociate themselves, another scene of collapsed excuse.
When the Hour rises, the guilty despair, furnishing the surah's earlier direct portrait of their final loss of hope.
The associators find no intercessors among their alleged partners and disavow them, closely complementing the focus's lack of recourse.
The deniers reject resurrection as a return after being lost in earth, identifying the earlier refusal that makes the focus's Day decisive.
Wrongdoers, gathered before their Lord, blame one another after the truth becomes manifest, but no defense changes the result.
The powerless and powerful exchange blame and conceal regret when they see punishment, showing futile post-verdict rationalization.
No burdened soul can carry another's burden, a personal-accountability principle supporting the focus's failed excuse.
The trumpet summons people from graves to their Lord, supplying the resurrection event presupposed by the focus.
The command to stop them because they will be questioned gives the judicial procedure that contrasts with the focus's no-benefit excuse.
All intercession belongs to God alone, setting the boundary against imagined final advocacy.
The people of the Fire dispute and appeal to their keepers, but their mutual accusations do not alter the established punishment.
When the Hour arrives unexpectedly, the associates they once claimed are absent and they have no escape.
Former close friends become enemies on that Day except the God-conscious, further collapsing worldly relational reliance.
They are told to enter the Fire because they forgot the meeting of their Day and worldly life deceived them; no exit or restored favor follows.
The removal of the covering on that Day makes sight acute, clarifying why late recognition cannot count as a timely response.
The Day of presentation leaves no secret hidden, giving the disclosure setting in which excuses lose force.
The question of where to flee when the final upheaval comes directly evokes the absence of escape.
The near punishment makes a person see what his hands sent ahead and causes the disbeliever to wish for nonexistence.
The blazing Fire is made manifest in the sequence of final unveiling, strengthening the Day-of-reckoning setting.
Graves are overturned in the final disclosure, preparing the personal accounting made explicit in 82:19.
